The city hired a man to remove the names from things that no longer existed.

It was not a prestigious job, but it came with a pension and a bicycle.

Every morning, Emil received a list: a demolished cinema, a drained pond, a street absorbed into a shopping complex. He would ride out with his tools and take down the signs. Brass plaques went into one sack, enamel into another. Stone required paperwork.

His predecessor had lasted forty-three years.

“Don’t get interested,” she told him on her last day. “That’s how you end up keeping things.”

For eleven months, Emil followed her advice.

He removed the name of a bakery without wondering about the bread. He unscrewed a sign reading MERCY LANE from a wall that now enclosed a private car park. He scraped the words PUBLIC BATHS from a window behind which accountants sat in rows, wearing headphones.

Then, on a Thursday in November, he was sent to remove the name of a bridge.

The bridge was still there.

He checked the work order.

**HALFPENNY BRIDGE. NAME OBSOLETE. REMOVE ALL MUNICIPAL REFERENCES.**

Below this, someone had added:

**Structure to remain.**

Emil leaned his bicycle against the railing.

The bridge crossed a narrow canal. There were weeds in the mortar and a glove on one of the posts, its fingers stiff with frost. Two brass plates bore the bridge’s name, one at either end.

An old woman stood in the middle, feeding nothing.

She had a paper bag. Every so often she reached into it and made a scattering motion, but Emil could see nothing falling.

“Birds gone?” he asked.

“Years ago.”

“What are you feeding?”

She folded the bag shut.

“Is that your business?”

“No,” he said. “Mine’s the signs.”

He showed her the work order. She read it carefully, holding the bottom of the page between two fingers.

“They stopped charging the halfpenny in 1906,” she said.

“That would explain it.”

“Would it?”

Emil looked at the bridge again. It was only a bridge, and the plates were held on by ordinary screws.

He took out his screwdriver.

“My husband proposed to me here,” the woman said.

He paused.

“I said no.”

“Oh.”

“Then I proposed to him here the following spring. He asked whether I was certain. I told him not to spoil it.”

Emil put the screwdriver into the first screw.

“What was his name?”

“Daniel.”

The screw was old and came free with a small cry.

That afternoon, instead of taking the brass to the depot, Emil brought it home.

He lived above a pharmacy in two rooms that smelled faintly of cardboard. He washed the plates in his kitchen sink and laid them on a towel.

HALFPENNY BRIDGE.

Without the bridge underneath them, the words looked oddly helpless.

He put one on the mantelpiece. The other went beneath his bed.

After that, he began to keep things.

A blue enamel street sign. A bronze dedication to a school garden. The wooden nameboard of a ferry that had been dismantled upriver.

He told himself he was saving the city disposal fees.

By February, he had nowhere to put his shoes.

By March, he was interested.

He started visiting the archives after work. He learned that Mercy Lane had been named not for the virtue but for a laundress who owned three houses there. He found a photograph of the public baths on opening day: children lined up with towels, a councillor holding scissors, everyone except the councillor blurred by movement.

He looked for Daniel.

There were too many Daniels.

When he next saw the woman on the bridge, he asked her surname.

She told him, then frowned.

“You haven’t put him on a list?”

“No.”

“Good. He hated committees.”

Emil admitted he had kept the signs.

“Both of them?”

“Yes.”

“What for?”

He had expected her to approve. He was embarrassed by how much he had expected it.

“I didn’t think they should be melted down.”

She looked towards the bare stone at the end of the bridge.

“Well,” she said, “they’re not doing much good in your flat.”

The following morning, Emil returned with his tools.

He fitted the first plate loosely, then went to the other end and fitted the second. Once both were straight, he tightened the screws.

A cyclist rang her bell. A delivery driver asked whether the canal path led to the hospital. Nothing else happened.

At the depot, Emil marked the work order incomplete.

“Reason?” asked the clerk.

“Bridge still in use.”

The clerk turned the form over, looking for a box that would accommodate this. Eventually she wrote it in the margin.

That evening, Emil began sorting the things in his flat.

Most could not go back. He knew that now. The ferry was gone; the bakery wall was rubble. He wrapped those signs carefully and wrote to the city museum.

But Mercy Lane’s wall remained.

He set the blue sign beside the door, put four screws in his coat pocket, and found his shoes.
